title: Elephant Paths to a Cloud Forest: Climbing Mt Ololokwe in Samburu
meta_title: Mt Ololokwe Hike: Sacred 2,000 m Summit, Worth the Climb
meta_description: Plan a Mt Ololokwe hike in Samburu: route from Sabache Camp, trail stats, best months, guides and what to pack for the long drive from Nairobi.
excerpt: A Mt Ololokwe hike climbs about 1,000 m of steep elephant paths from Sabache Camp to a cedar-forested summit at around 2,000 m. Here is the route, timing, season and kit, plus how to get there from Nairobi.
featured_image_alt: Mt Ololokwe hike country: hazy hills of Samburu, northern Kenya, seen across a wide valley
content:
Rising sheer out of the thorn plains just north of Archers Post, Ol Donyo Sabache is the flat-topped mountain a Mt Ololokwe hike climbs. Expect roughly 1,000 m of steep elephant paths from Sabache Camp to a cool cedar forest on top at about 2,000 m, with most fit hikers reaching the summit in two to four hours.

Finding the mountain is easy; it fills the windscreen long before you arrive. The real challenges are the heat on the lower slopes, the long road from Nairobi and planning guides, water and camping. Below are the route, trail stats, best months, kit and training.

Quick Facts

  • Location: Samburu County, beside the Isiolo–Marsabit highway, about 27 km north of Archers Post.
  • Summit: about 2,000 m, a forested table top with sheer cliffs on every side.
  • Start point: Sabache Camp, where every Mt Ololokwe hike begins, at roughly 1,000 m.
  • Ascent time: 2-4 hours up; a full day out is usually 5-8 hours.
  • Distance from Nairobi: about 340 km by road, with no public transport to the trailhead.
  • Wildlife: a roosting and nesting site for the Critically Endangered Rüppell's vulture.

Where Is Mt Ololokwe and How Far Is It From Nairobi?

Mt Ololokwe stands in Samburu County, northern Kenya, about 340 km from Nairobi by road. It sits right beside the tarmac heading north to Marsabit, so the drive is long but simple. You will need your own car or a group trip, because no matatu reaches the camp.

Driving from Nairobi

Leave Nairobi on Thika Road and follow the highway north to Karatina, then take the Nanyuki road. Carry on through Nanyuki, Timau and Isiolo to Archers Post. About 27 km beyond Archers Post, a signed 4 km dirt track turns left to Sabache Camp at the foot of the cliffs. Allow six hours or more with stops, which is why nearly everyone treats a Mt Ololokwe hike as a weekend rather than a day trip.

Can you get there by public transport?

Buses run up the A2 towards Isiolo and Marsabit, but none stop at Sabache Camp, and the track in crosses elephant country. For a Mt Ololokwe hike, use a private car, a hired driver or a group trip.

Mt Ololokwe Hike Trail Stats

This climb is short in distance but steep, climbing about 1,000 m with little shade on the lower half. These figures come from local hiking sources and vary with pace and route choice.

What Is the Route Like From Sabache to the Summit?

The Mt Ololokwe hike climbs the eastern side of the mountain on paths first trodden by elephants, then cattle and people. It is steepest in the first two hours, eases at a series of rock clearings and finishes on a flat, forested plateau with cliff-edge viewpoints.

The lower slopes: thorn bush and heat

From the dry riverbed at Sabache Camp, the path heads straight into acacia, commiphora and candelabra euphorbia. This is the hottest, most exposed stretch of the whole route, and hikers commonly stop every 10 to 15 minutes. Elephant dung and bark-stripped trees show who made the trail, so stay close to your guide.

The first clearings and the Cat and Mouse rocks

Rock slabs partway up give the first wide views north across the plains towards Laisamis. Look for the two formations locals call the cat and the mouse, and the Mathews Range to the north-east. Along the way you may pass a stone cairn where first-time visitors traditionally add a stone.

The table top forest

The reward at the end of a Mt Ololokwe hike is a different world: cedar and podocarpus, strangler figs and lichen hanging from the branches like grey beards. Permanent springs on top feed small streams, which is why elephants and herders' cattle climb up in dry spells. The plateau also holds a rare cycad found only in this part of Kenya.

The cliff edge and the vultures

Because the summit is wooded, the best views are from the cliff edges. The south-western rim looks down on the highway running back towards Isiolo, while the south-eastern edge takes in the Mathews Range. Pause here on any Mt Ololokwe hike and watch the air below: according to Nature Kenya's Key Biodiversity Area profile, these cliffs are a roosting and nesting site for the Critically Endangered Rüppell's vulture and the rarely seen Taita falcon.

When Is the Best Time for a Mt Ololokwe Hike?

The drier months, roughly January to February and June to October, give the safest footing and clearest views. The long rains (about March to May) and short rains (about October to December) bring slippery rock and cloud, though the lower slopes stay hot all year.

Whatever the month, start a Mt Ololokwe hike early. Leaving camp at first light gets you through the exposed bush before the sun is high and into the cool forest by mid-morning. Afternoon starts are a common mistake that turn a moderate climb into a gruelling one.

In November and December, the short rains can bring heavy showers to Samburu. If you plan a Mt Ololokwe hike then, pack a waterproof layer and allow extra time on the descent, when wet rock is at its most slippery.

Do You Need a Guide, and What About Fees?

Yes, book a local Samburu guide for any Mt Ololokwe hike. The trail crosses community land, wildlife including elephants and buffalo uses the same paths, and the mountain is sacred to the Samburu people.

Respecting a sacred mountain

Samburu elders climb Ololokwe to pray and make offerings, especially before major events, and the mountain has long served as a shrine. On a Mt Ololokwe hike, ask your guide before photographing people or sites on top, stay on the paths and carry out all rubbish.

Fees and permits

The mountain lies in community conservancy country near Namunyak, Kalama and West Gate, not in a national park, so charges are set locally. Published figures disagree, so confirm current conservancy, guide and camping fees with Sabache Camp or the conservancy before you travel.

Can you camp on the summit?

Yes. Many people turn a Mt Ololokwe hike into an overnight trip on the plateau, usually after a night at Sabache Camp, which also takes campers with their own tents. Summit campers must be self-sufficient. Nights on top are cool and windy, so pack a warm layer even though the plains below bake.

What to Wear and Pack for the Climb

Pack for two climates on a Mt Ololokwe hike: hot, dusty bush at the bottom and a cool, sometimes misty forest on top. The basics are grippy boots, plenty of water, sun protection and a warm layer, plus a headlamp if you plan to camp or start before dawn.

  • Boots with grip: the elephant paths are steep, rocky and loose in places. A pair like the Quechua waterproof hiking boot gives ankle support and a lugged sole for the descent.
  • Good socks: long, hot climbs mean sweaty feet. Merino wool hiking socks handle heat and help prevent blisters.
  • Water, and lots of it: carry at least 3 litres per person for a day climb. A 3L hydration backpack lets you sip without stopping on the steep sections.
  • Sun cover: a wide-brim safari sun hat, sunglasses and sunscreen for the exposed lower slopes.
  • Light and layers: a rechargeable headlamp for early starts or a night on top, a fleece and a rain shell.

Pro Tips

  • Sleep at Sabache Camp the night before so your Mt Ololokwe hike starts at first light.
  • Fill every bottle in Isiolo or at camp; do not rely on the summit springs for drinking water without treating it.
  • Keep a fleece and rain shell in your pack, even when it is over 30°C at the bottom.

How to Train for the Climb From Nairobi

Train for a Mt Ololokwe hike with steep, sustained climbing in heat rather than long distances. Two or three hill hikes in the month before your trip, carrying the same pack and water you will use on the day, prepare your legs and show you how much you drink.

  1. Start with a forest walk: a long loop at Karura Forest tests your boots and socks on easy ground.
  2. Add steady climbing: the ridge walk on the Ngong Hills builds stamina on repeated ups and downs.
  3. Rehearse the heat and the steepness: Mt Longonot or Mt Suswa in the Rift Valley are the closest match to the dry, exposed lower slopes.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does the Mt Ololokwe hike take?

Climbing Ololokwe usually takes two to four hours from Sabache Camp to the summit plateau, depending on fitness, heat and how often you stop. With time to explore the forest and cliff viewpoints on top, most groups spend five to eight hours on the mountain in total.

Is Mt Ololokwe hard to climb for a beginner?

A Mt Ololokwe hike gains about 1,000 m steeply, so it suits beginners who already manage Ngong Hills or Longonot comfortably. The path is not technical and needs no ropes, but the heat on the lower slopes is tiring. Start at first light, go with a local guide, rest often and carry plenty of water.

Can I do a Mt Ololokwe hike as a day trip from Nairobi?

Climbing Ololokwe as a same-day return from Nairobi is not realistic for most people. The drive is about 340 km each way, often six hours or more, which leaves no safe time to climb in daylight. Plan a weekend instead: drive up on Friday or Saturday morning, sleep at Sabache Camp, climb at dawn and drive home afterwards.

Is there water on top of Ololokwe?

Ololokwe has permanent springs on its summit plateau, which is why elephants and cattle climb up during dry spells. Do not plan on them as your drinking supply, though. Carry at least 3 litres per person for a day climb, and if you camp on top, bring a filter or purification tablets.

Final Thoughts

Heat at the bottom, cedar shade at the top and vultures circling the cliffs in between: that is the shape of a day on this sacred Samburu mountain.

Go in a dry month, sleep at the base, start at first light with a local guide and carry more water than feels necessary, and a Mt Ololokwe hike becomes one of the most rewarding climbs in northern Kenya. Pick a weekend, sort boots and water first, then head up the A2.
